title: Psalm 32: The Happiness of the Forgiven
summary: David pronounces a blessing on the person whose sins are forgiven and covered, then tells what it was like to hide his sin: his body wasted under God's heavy hand until he confessed and was forgiven. He urges the godly to pray while God may be found, God himself promises to teach the way, and the psalm ends with a call for the upright to rejoice.
story: Psalm 31 ended by telling the faithful to be strong and to hope in the LORD. Psalm 32 takes up a question that such hope has to face: what happens when the trouble is my own sin? Many psalms cry out against enemies; this one looks inward. It is one of the church's seven penitential psalms (with Psalms 6, 38, 51, 102, 130, and 143), a grouping that goes back at least to the sixth-century writer Cassiodorus. It also carries the first occurrence in the Psalter of the heading Maskil. Paul quotes its opening verses in Romans 4 as proof that God has always counted people righteous apart from their works, which makes this short psalm one of the Old Testament's clearest statements of grace.
historical:
The heading attributes the psalm to David, and many readers, ancient and modern, connect it with his adultery with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah, and with the long silence before Nathan confronted him (2 Samuel 11 and 12). Psalm 51 carries that setting in its heading; Psalm 32 does not name any event, and the link is an inference from the content. Scholars who doubt that David wrote the psalms under his name read Psalm 32 as a thanksgiving song composed for any forgiven worshiper to sing, perhaps at the temple after an offering. Either reading takes seriously what the psalm describes: a person who hid wrongdoing, suffered for it in body and spirit, confessed, and was forgiven.

Maskil is a technical term in the headings of thirteen psalms. Its meaning is uncertain. It comes from a root meaning to be wise or to have insight, and suggestions include a teaching psalm, a skillful or artful song, or a psalm that makes one wise. The same root appears in verse 8, I will instruct you, which fits the teaching sense well.
cultural:
The psalm assumes the Old Testament's rich vocabulary for wrongdoing. Transgression means rebellion, a breach of trust or a crossing of a boundary. Sin means missing the mark. Iniquity means twistedness, and can refer both to the wrong done and to the guilt that follows. The speaker uses all three, as if to say that however his wrong is described, it has been dealt with. The verbs for forgiveness match: lifted away, covered, not counted. To count something against someone was the language of a ledger or a legal charge.

The description of physical suffering in verses 3 and 4 draws on the dry heat of the eastern Mediterranean summer, when streams fail and plants wither. Ancient Israelites did not divide body and soul the way modern readers often do, and the psalm treats guilt as something felt in the bones. Verse 9 uses a familiar farm image: horses and mules had to be steered with bit and bridle because they would not come willingly. The contrast is with a person who hears counsel and follows it freely.
literary: The psalm opens with two beatitudes (blessing statements beginning Blessed is), then tells a story in verses 3 to 5, with a sharp turn between silence and confession. The word Selah (verses 4, 5, and 7) is probably a musical or liturgical marker, perhaps a pause; its exact meaning is unknown. In verses 8 and 9 the speaker changes. Most interpreters hear God speaking, promising to instruct and watch over, though some think the forgiven psalmist now teaches others. Verse 10 draws the wisdom contrast between the sorrows of the wicked and the loving devotion that surrounds the one who trusts, and verse 11 widens into a call to worship. The psalm moves from private confession to public teaching to shared joy.

outline.t: The misery of silence and the relief of confession
Pray while God may be found; he is a hiding place
God's promise to instruct, and a warning against stubbornness
Sorrows for the wicked, steadfast love for the trusting, joy for the upright

doctrines.note: Forgiveness here is a gift received, not a wage earned: sin is lifted, covered, and not counted. Paul uses verses 1 and 2 to show that God credits righteousness apart from works, and that David already knew this grace.
The psalm contrasts two ways of handling sin. Silence wastes the body and dries the spirit; confession brings forgiveness at once. Repentance is not self-punishment but telling the truth to God.

Using three words for wrongdoing, the psalm shows sin as rebellion, failure, and distortion, and it shows how hidden sin corrodes a person from within. Sin is serious enough to need God's covering, and God is gracious enough to give it.

words.note: Esher, usually rendered blessed, describes the happy, flourishing condition of a person rightly related to God. It is the same word that opens Psalm 1. There it belongs to the one who delights in God's law; here, strikingly, it belongs to the one whose failures are forgiven. The Psalter's happiness rests finally on grace.

Kasah, to cover. In verse 1 God covers sin; in verse 5 the psalmist says he did not cover (hide) his iniquity. The same verb works both ways. When a person covers his own sin, it festers; when he uncovers it before God, God covers it. The word sits close to the language of atonement in Israel's sacrificial system.

Nasa, to lift or carry, here meaning to forgive. The picture is of a burden lifted off and carried away. It is the same verb used in Exodus 34:7, where the LORD describes himself as forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin. Forgiveness in the Old Testament is God bearing away what we could not carry.

Chashav, to count or reckon. In verse 2 the LORD does not count iniquity against a person. The verb is used in Genesis 15:6, where Abraham's faith was counted to him as righteousness, and Paul brings the two texts together in Romans 4. It is bookkeeping language turned into a picture of mercy.

christ: Paul quotes verses 1 and 2 in Romans 4:6-8 to show that God has always justified the ungodly by grace through faith, not by works. He pairs David with Abraham: both were counted righteous by God's gift. The New Testament explains how God can cover sin without ignoring it: Christ bore sin in his own body on the cross (1 Peter 2:24), so the covering of Psalm 32 finds its ground in his atoning death. The psalm's promise that confession brings forgiveness is echoed in 1 John 1:9. Christians have long read this psalm as one of the clearest Old Testament witnesses to the gospel of grace, not because it predicts the cross, but because it describes the same mercy the cross secures.
questions: The psalmist describes the physical toll of keeping silent about sin. Have you seen hidden guilt affect your body, your sleep, or your relationships?
Why do you think confession is so hard, when the psalm says forgiveness came as soon as he spoke?
Verse 9 warns against being like a horse or mule that must be steered with a bit. What is the difference between obeying God under pressure and following him freely?
